work.text: Tao-chi's painting of the grotto, done at the peak of his [artistic] powers around 1700, is one of his most sumptuous [masterpieces]. Following an earlier composition by Shen Chou (1427-1509), Tao-chi painted as if he were reenacting the [cosmic] processes of creation; by building up layers of energized brushwork in flowery hues of sky blue, pale green, orange, and fuchsia, he transformed Shen Chou's topographical [likeness] into a glowing image redolent of nature's procreative power.

work.text: The picture is typical of Shih-t'ao's most polished commissioned works, and clearly represents the artist at his most professional.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Peach Blossom Spring: Gardens and Flowers in Chinese Paintings
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: Chang Kung's Grotto, a famous scenic spot, and once the abode of Chang Tao-ling (Chang Kung, second century A.D.), a Taoist immortal and patriarch of the Taoist church, is located near Lake T'ai in Kiangsu Province … According to Taoist beliefs such grottos are wellsprings of nature's creative force and offer the potential for rejuvenation and renewal.

source.author: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
source.title: Tao-chi (Shih-t’ao), Outing to Chang Kung’s Grotto
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Notable Acquisitions 1982–1983 (Internet Archive scan)

moment.text: It is thanks to Wolfgang Bauer that we now realize how significant the idea of the grotto was to Taoist thought. The cave symbolized a passageway, through the rocks, through space and time; and the passage was a journey, toward [enlightenment] and happiness, toward renewal and rebirth.

source.author: Richard M. Barnhart
source.title: Peach Blossom Spring: Gardens and Flowers in Chinese Paintings
source.publisher: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Internet Archive scan)

matters.text: No one is in Chang Kung's Grotto, But from inside Chang Kung's Grotto a spring breeze arises. … When most people talk about it they are always rather vague, Yet I must paint both its spirit and principle. … Cave, oh cave, now it is in my painting

matters.text: Da Dizi was taken when Shitao renounced his Buddhist faith and turned to Daoism. It was also the name he used for his home in Yangzhou
